subtopic: Planning a trip on a budget
subtype: Approach: going along with the loudest friend [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Seema. On the group call Pankaj said, “Adventure park, day two. Best rides, my cousin went, it's amazing.” He said it as if it were already booked. Everyone said “yes!” and “so cool!” The ticket was 900 rupees. Nobody said the price out loud. My stomach tightened, because my trip money had been counted carefully, and 900 was more than I'd set aside for the whole day. I typed “sounds great” and closed the call. I found out later that Rekha, who sits behind me, had done exactly the same. We both spent that evening quietly working out what to skip. I didn't object because everyone seemed so happy, and I didn't want to be the person who spoils it. Looking back, one sentence, what does it cost, would have saved us both.

qa.q: How much was the ticket for the adventure park?
Why did Seema type sounds great?
qa.a: Seema did not want to be the person who spoils the mood and felt unable to object, though Seema was anxious about the cost.

qa.q: What could the group have done differently?
qa.a: They could have asked what each activity costs and agreed a shared limit before choosing, so nobody has to stay silent.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see the plan?
qa.a: Pankaj probably thinks everyone is excited and does not realise the price is troubling others.

grounding: The group accepts one boy's idea of a costly adventure park without discussing money, and two members quietly struggle to afford it.
